concept.name: Vega hedge
concept.definition: An options-hedging technique that neutralizes a position's vega - the change in option premium for a one-percentage-point change in implied volatility - so the book is insulated from shifts in the market's volatility expectations.
concept.intuition: Options get more expensive when expected volatility rises, even if prices don't move; a vega hedge makes your position indifferent to that repricing.
concept.mechanics: Vega measures premium change per 1% (100-basis-point) change in implied volatility; it is larger for longer-dated options. Because the underlying has zero vega, vega must be hedged with offsetting option positions, after which delta (and possibly gamma) is re-neutralized; vega hedges across maturities leave term-structure-of-volatility risk.
concept.formula: Position vega = sum over positions of (quantity * multiplier * vega_i); offset with an options position whose aggregate vega equals -position vega.
concept.failure_modes: Implied volatility is not directly tradable, so vega hedges rely on other options whose own prices embed supply-demand distortions; vega also changes with price, time, and vol level, so the hedge decays, and short-dated and long-dated implied vols do not move in lockstep.
concept.misconceptions: A vega-neutral book is not immune to volatility: it is hedged against a uniform 1% implied-vol shift, not against realized volatility gaps or non-parallel shifts across the volatility surface.
concept.example: A trader long a 12-month call with vega 0.15 (gaining about $0.30 if implied vol rises 2%) shorts enough nearer-dated options totaling -0.15 vega per share equivalent, flattening the book's response to a volatility spike.

citations.source: The Options Industry Council (OIC), Options Education: Vega
